body:
What is a launch vehicle?

A launch vehicle is a rocket designed to carry a spacecraft or another payload from Earth and place it on a suitable trajectory. When the destination is an Earth orbit, the vehicle must give the spacecraft sufficient speed in the required direction to remain in orbit. The spacecraft then separates from the launch vehicle and carries out its own mission.

The payload is the object being transported. It may be an Earth-observation satellite, a communication satellite, a navigation satellite, a scientific spacecraft or a combination of smaller satellites. Payload mass is usually expressed in kilograms or tonnes, where 1 tonne equals 1,000 kg.

A launch vehicle and a satellite perform different functions. The rocket provides the major acceleration needed for launch and initial orbital insertion. The satellite carries instruments, communication equipment and other systems needed to perform its mission after separation. Some satellites also have their own propulsion systems for changing or maintaining their orbits.

How does a rocket reach space?

A rocket produces thrust by expelling high-speed gases in one direction. The reaction force pushes the rocket in the opposite direction. This is an application of Newton's third law of motion: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. A rocket does not need surrounding air to push against and can therefore operate in space.

Reaching a sufficient height is not enough to establish an orbit. The spacecraft also needs the required sideways velocity. Earth's gravity continuously pulls an orbiting spacecraft towards Earth, but its forward motion allows it to keep moving around the planet instead of falling directly to the surface.

Why are rockets divided into stages?

Most orbital launch vehicles have several stages. Each stage contains a propulsion system and contributes to accelerating the vehicle. After a stage has completed its useful work, it can be separated so that the remaining rocket no longer carries unnecessary mass.

A strap-on booster is an additional rocket motor attached to the main vehicle to provide extra thrust, especially during the early part of flight. Strap-on boosters should not automatically be counted as separate sequential stages. This distinction is important when comparing PSLV, GSLV and LVM3.

Orbits determine the launch requirement

Different satellites need different orbits. An orbit is the path followed by a spacecraft under the influence of gravity. The required orbital altitude, inclination and shape influence the launch vehicle's payload capacity.

Low Earth Orbit

Low Earth Orbit (LEO) consists of orbits relatively close to Earth. Earth-observation satellites, many scientific satellites and several communication constellations operate in this region. A satellite in LEO generally completes an orbit much faster than Earth completes one rotation.

Polar and Sun-Synchronous Orbits

A polar orbit passes over or near Earth's polar regions. As Earth rotates beneath the spacecraft, successive passes can observe different parts of the planet.

A Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO) is a specially selected near-polar orbit in which the orbital plane changes gradually so that the spacecraft crosses a given location at approximately the same local solar time. Similar lighting conditions are useful for comparing Earth-observation images obtained on different days. The expression Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit (SSPO) is commonly used in Indian launch-vehicle specifications.

Not every polar orbit is Sun-synchronous, and not every satellite in LEO follows a polar orbit.

Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit and Geostationary Orbit

A Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) is a highly elliptical orbit used as an intermediate step towards certain high-altitude orbits. Its closest point to Earth is called perigee, while its farthest point is called apogee.

After being placed in GTO, a satellite can use its own propulsion system to raise the perigee, change the orbital inclination and reach its intended operational orbit. The launch vehicle therefore does not necessarily place the satellite directly into its final orbit.

A geosynchronous orbit has an orbital period equal to Earth's rotation period relative to the stars. A geostationary orbit (GEO) is a special circular geosynchronous orbit in Earth's equatorial plane, moving in the same direction as Earth's rotation. A geostationary satellite appears fixed over a particular longitude. Its altitude is approximately 35,786 km above Earth's surface.

GTO is not GEO. GTO is an elliptical transfer orbit. GEO is a circular, equatorial operational orbit. Successful injection into GTO does not, by itself, establish that the satellite has reached its final geostationary position.

How payload capacity is stated

A launch vehicle's payload capacity is not one fixed number for every mission. The mass it can deliver depends on the destination orbit and the mission's requirements. For example, a rocket may carry considerably more mass into LEO than into GTO because reaching a higher-energy transfer orbit generally requires additional acceleration.

Indian launch vehicles are therefore often described using two related facts: their payload class, such as small, medium or heavy, and the destination orbit for which a particular mass capacity is quoted.

Prelims focus

  • A launch vehicle transports a payload and provides the acceleration needed for launch and orbital insertion.
  • Rocket propulsion works by expelling gases and does not require atmospheric air.
  • LEO is a low-altitude orbital region; a polar orbit is defined by its path near the poles.
  • Sun-synchronous orbits provide approximately consistent local solar time for repeated observations.
  • GTO is an elliptical transfer orbit; GEO is a circular equatorial orbit about 35,786 km above Earth.
  • Trap: Reaching space, entering Earth orbit and reaching a satellite's final operational orbit are not necessarily the same event.

[NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6 Geography, Chapter 1, The Earth in the Solar System, printed pp. 1–5, 2018–19; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 17, Stars and the Solar System, printed pp. 226–233, 2018–19; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 10, Gravitation, printed pp. 132–135, 2018–19; ISRO, Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mark II, sections on the cryogenic upper stage and orbital insertion, accessed 4 November 2026.]

title: Launch Vehicles and Orbits: Foundations for Understanding Indian Rockets

body:
Purpose and main characteristics

PSLV stands for Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle. Developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), it became one of India's principal launch vehicles for Earth-observation, scientific and other satellite missions. It is often described as ISRO's workhorse because of its extensive use across many missions.

PSLV was designed primarily for placing satellites into polar and Sun-synchronous orbits. However, its capabilities are not restricted to those orbits. It has also launched navigation satellites, scientific spacecraft and missions that subsequently travelled towards the Moon, Mars or the Sun–Earth L1 region.

The 4 propulsion stages of PSLV

The most distinctive structural fact about PSLV is its sequence of alternating solid and liquid propulsion stages.

  1. First stage, PS1: Solid. The large solid rocket motor provides the substantial thrust needed during liftoff and early ascent. Depending on the variant, additional solid strap-on boosters may assist it.
  2. Second stage, PS2: Liquid. A liquid-propellant stage powered by a Vikas engine continues accelerating the vehicle after the first stage separates.
  3. Third stage, PS3: Solid. Another solid rocket motor contributes further acceleration during the upper part of the ascent.
  4. Fourth stage, PS4: Liquid. The final liquid-propellant stage provides controlled acceleration for placing satellites into the required orbit. Its ability to support precise orbital insertion is particularly useful for missions carrying multiple satellites.

PSLV does not use a cryogenic upper stage. Its fourth stage uses liquid propellants, but liquid propulsion and cryogenic propulsion are not identical terms. Cryogenic systems involve propellants stored at extremely low temperatures; PSLV's liquid stages use other propellants.

PSLV variants and strap-on boosters

Different PSLV configurations provide flexibility for payloads with different launch requirements. The principal variants differ in the number of solid strap-on boosters attached to the first stage.

  • PSLV-CA: Core Alone configuration with 0 strap-on boosters.
  • PSLV-DL: Configuration with 2 strap-on boosters.
  • PSLV-QL: Configuration with 4 strap-on boosters.
  • PSLV-XL: Configuration with 6 extended strap-on boosters.

These configurations do not change PSLV's basic count of 4 sequential stages. A mission identifier such as PSLV-C57 identifies a particular launch; it does not mean that the rocket has 57 stages.

Payload capacity and suitable orbits

ISRO's vehicle specifications give PSLV a capacity of approximately 1,750 kg to a 600 km Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit. Its published capability also includes approximately 1,425 kg to a sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit, which is different from the full GTO normally associated with GSLV missions.

These figures explain PSLV's association with medium-class Earth-observation satellites and missions carrying several smaller spacecraft. Multiple satellites may be released during one flight when their required orbits and the vehicle's mission plan are compatible.

Important PSLV missions and dates

DateMissionImportance
20 September 1993PSLV-D1First developmental flight; unsuccessful.
15 October 1994PSLV-D2First successful PSLV flight.
22 October 2008PSLV-C11Launched Chandrayaan-1, India's first lunar mission.
5 November 2013PSLV-C25Launched the Mars Orbiter Mission, also called Mangalyaan.
28 September 2015PSLV-C30Launched AstroSat, India's multiwavelength space observatory.
15 February 2017PSLV-C37Successfully launched 104 satellites in one flight.
2 September 2023PSLV-C57Launched Aditya-L1, India's solar-observation mission.
30 December 2024PSLV-C60Launched the SpaDeX spacecraft for space-docking experiments.

PSLV-C37 carried 104 satellites in total: a Cartosat-2 series Earth-observation satellite and 103 co-passengers. The figure does not mean that all 104 satellites belonged to India.

Chandrayaan-1 and the Mars Orbiter Mission illustrate another important distinction. PSLV provided their initial launch and Earth-orbit insertion. Subsequent spacecraft propulsion and orbital manoeuvres enabled the journeys towards the Moon and Mars.

Recent PSLV outcomes: status at the content cutoff

Launch records must distinguish the reputation of a vehicle family from the result of an individual flight. On 18 May 2025, PSLV-C61 carrying EOS-09 did not accomplish its intended mission following an anomaly in the third stage. On 12 January 2026, PSLV-C62 carrying EOS-N1 encountered an anomaly towards the end of the PS3 stage.

These are reported mission outcomes, not evidence that the basic PSLV stage configuration has changed. The descriptions above reflect information published by ISRO and available up to 4 November 2026.

Prelims focus

  • PSLV stands for Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle.
  • It has 4 stages in the sequence solid, liquid, solid, liquid.
  • PSLV-CA, DL, QL and XL use 0, 2, 4 and 6 strap-on boosters respectively.
  • Its published capacity is about 1,750 kg to a 600 km Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit.
  • Chandrayaan-1, Mangalyaan and Aditya-L1 were launched using PSLV.
  • PSLV-C37 launched 104 satellites on 15 February 2017.
  • Trap: PSLV is not limited to polar missions and does not use a cryogenic upper stage.

[ISRO, PSLV, sections Vehicle Specifications, Strap-on Boosters and Technical Specification, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, List of PSLV Launches, mission records for 1993–2026, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, PSLV-C37 Successfully Launches 104 Satellites in a Single Flight, 15 February 2017; ISRO, PSLV-C61/EOS-09 Mission, mission update of 18 May 2025; ISRO, PSLV-C62/EOS-N1 Mission, January 2026 mission update; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 17, Stars and the Solar System, printed pp. 229–233, 2018–19.]
